Suliga , Glennys R. Farrar View a PDF of the paper titled Lightest and heaviest nuclei as keys to the origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays, by Anna M. Suliga and Glennys R. Farrar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has been a long-standing mystery. A unique feature of UHECRs originating in binary neutron star mergers (BNSMs) is two distinct populations of light elements -- those directly accelerated in the jets, and photo-disintegration products of massive nuclei accelerated in the bulk outflow. We show that Pierre Auger Observatory spectrum and composition data confirm the existence of the predicted two populations at $\geq \!7.2\sigma$ significance, having rigidity ($R\equiv E/Ze$) cutoffs agreeing with prior estimates. The data also favor 5-10% of UHECRs originating as r-process nuclei, a signature of a BNSM origin. Our results provide strong evidence that UHECRs are produced by merging neutron stars, and show how UHECRs and UHE-neutrinos elucidate otherwise inaccessible aspects of neutron star mergers. Comments: 22+11 pages, 3+4 figures. Under review in Science Subjects: High Energy Astrophysical Phenomena (astro-ph.HE) ; High Energy Phy

Vassilakis and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Understanding the Universe's large-scale distribution of dark matter is a central objective in the era of precision cosmology. A key technique for the study of dark matter is weak gravitational lensing: a phenomenon where light from distant galaxies is sheared as it passes through the gravitational field of a massive object, like a galaxy cluster. This shear, which manifests as a slight (weak) distortion of shapes over thousands of galaxies, allows astrophysicists to infer the distribution of total matter, including both luminous and dark matter. Obtaining a mass distribution from a catalog of galaxy shears involves reconstructing the convergence ($\kappa$), the projected surface mass density divided by the critical surface density for the lens-source system. Feedback welcome through GitHub in the TPAC 2026 breakout session proposal . Purpose This policy sets expectations and requirements for any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for standards work at W3C. It builds on the Use of Large Language Models in Standards Work document published by W3C’s Advisory Board. In general, a variety of tools are used in W3C to help with the development of technical specifications and best practices, including for authoring, versioning, validation, analysis, cross-linking, and automation. These tools are valued when they improve collaboration. Due to their ability to generate content at will, AI tools may hinder collaboration when their usage is unsanctioned or without guardrails. This policy is based upon the principle that every W3C contribution must be attributable to a human contributor who has reviewed and approved its content before publication, understands its substance, and accepts responsibility for its relevance, meaningfulness, correctness, quality, security, scope, provenance, and compliance with other applicable W3C policies . AI tools may be used to assist with a contribution, but may not be treated as contributors or act as unsupervised participants in W3C work. These are special-cased by the Python compiler to allow the use of new Python features in modules containing the future statement before the release in which the feature becomes standard. While these future statements are given additional special meaning by the Python compiler, they are still executed like any other import statement and the __future__ exists and is handled by the import system the same way any other Python module would be. This design serves three purposes: To avoid confusing existing tools that analyze import statements and expect to find the modules they’re importing. To document when incompatible changes were introduced, and when they will be — or were — made mandatory. This is a form of executable documentation, and can be inspected programmatically via importing __future__ and examining its contents. To ensure that future statements run under releases prior to Python 2.1 at least yield runtime exceptions (the import of __future__ will fail, because there was no module of that name prior to 2.1). The Mystic Link Trail is a conceptual effort to link together various green spaces to form a route from Ward Reservation in Andover, MA, US down to Boston, ending at the wharf where the Constitution is docked. See the main website for all the details. In its present form, it’s a little over 32 miles long. We have a relation defined in Open Streetmap to gather all the relevant ways, and a downloadable GPX file with mile markers for easy on-device following. Note that there are some areas where bicycles are not permitted, so there will be an alternate relation so riders can bypass some minor sections. Polyscias gymnocarpa `ohe`ohe View Profile FWS Focus overview characteristics geography timeline information & media contact Overview Polyscias gymnocarpa, a member of the Araliaceae (ginseng) family, is a tree 2.5 to 10 m (8 to 33 ft) tall, either hairless or with fuzzy, short-lived hairs on young leaves and flower clusters. The leaves are 30 to 55 cm (12 to 22 in) long with 7 to 21 leathery, oval to elliptic leaflets per leaf. Each leaflet is 7 to 18 cm (2.8 to 7.1 in) long and 3 to 8 cm (1.2 to 3.1 in) wide and is folded upward along the midvein. The flowers are usually arranged in threes or in an umbrella-shaped arrangement. Petals are 4 to 8 mm (0.2 to 0.3 in) long and usually number 5 or 6 per flower; with an equal number of stamens. The ovary has 3 or 4 sections and appears placed atop the receptacle (base of the flower) in a superior position, due to the expansion of the ovary disk (outgrowth of the receptacle) and the reduction of the hypanthium (basal portion of the flower). Fruits are purplish, oval or top-shaded drupes, 6 to 12 mm (0.2 to 0.5 in) long, that enclose a papery endocarp and single seeds. pages.text: A 50-day voyage to the kingdom of ice | National Geographic Premium ANIMALS FROM THE VAULT A 50-day voyage to the kingdom of ice National Geographic joined an expedition to understand the mysterious creatures of the ice-locked southern continent. pages.text: A Blessing in Disguise: The Long-Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old-Age Male Longevity | NBER Skip to main content A Blessing in Disguise: The Long-Term Effects of Childhood Exposure to the Boll Weevil on Old-Age Male Longevity Hamid Noghanibehambari & Jason Fletcher Share X LinkedIn Facebook Bluesky Threads Email Link Working Paper 36031 DOI 10.3386/w36031 Issue Date November 2026 The infamous agricultural pest, the boll weevil, spread across southern US counties between 1892 and 1920. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. We show that the estimated effects are robust across a wide array of specifications, are not driven by sociodemographic and socioeconomic compositional change in the final sample, and are not associated with pre-existing trends in the outcome. Further, we find larger impacts among Blacks, children of lower educated mothers, whose fathers work in the farming industry, and those born in high cotton intensity counties. pages.text: A bold plan to save Africa’s shrinking giraffe herds | National Geographic By Joshua Foer Photographs by Ami Vitale 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. Of all the large African mammals that wildlife veterinarian Pete Morkel has had to capture over his career—lions, forest elephants, white rhinos— giraffes are the most stressful. “With other animals, you’re trying to give just enough anesthetic to immobilize them, but with a giraffe, we use a total overdose to chemically knock them off their feet,” the sun-leathered 59-year-old tells me as I stalk him stalking a two-year-old female giraffe somewhere in the Nigerien bush, about 60 miles east of Niamey, Niger’s capital. He is wearing a camo hat and a pair of torn, purple-checkered boxers that he’s been wearing as shorts for the past several days. ( Giraffes Seen Feasting on Skeleton—Here's Why) Morkel has loaded his dart gun with a dose of etorphine, an opioid about 6,000 times more powerful than morphine. Once it penetrates the giraffe’s skin, he and his team will have just minutes to chase down the animal, tackle her, and inject her neck with an antidote to keep her from dying. If she can be successfully captured and survive a 500-mile translocation across Niger, she’ll become one of eight founding “Adams” and “Eves” of a new population of one of the world’s rarest wild mammals. pages.title: A Brief History of Banned Books in America
pages.description: Attempts to restrict what kids in school can read are on the rise. But American book banning started with the Puritans, 140 years before the United States
pages.text: A Brief History of Banned Books in America Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report The New English Canaan by Thomas Morton criticized the Puritan government in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz The American Library Association reports that 2022 saw more attempts to have books removed from schools and public libraries than in any prior year this century—indeed, it documented nearly twice as many attempted bans in 2022 than in 2021. Notably, the common thread in these aggressive efforts is the subject that binds the most-challenged titles: Most of them address themes of LGBT+ identity or gender expression. On our latest episode of the Smithsonian magazine podcast “There’s More to That,” I talk with journalist Colleen Connolly about Thomas Morton’s New English Canaan , the first book ever to be suppressed in North America. What did the Puritans find so threatening about it, and how has this book echoed through subsequent centuries? Then I’m joined by Carla Hayden, the librarian of Congress, for a wide-ranging conversation about the history of book bans in the United States, how a resurgent wave of book bans in many states differs from those of prior eras and why organized attempts to prevent specific people from reading specific books usually fail. pages.text: A Brief History of Bulgogi, Korea's Most Delicious Export (Recipe) Skip to main content Bulgogi is a classic Korean dish of thinly sliced, marinated beef. 4kodiak/iStock Peter Serpico, the Seoul-born chef and namesake of the contemporary American restaurant Serpico in Philadelphia, knows good bulgogi . Like clockwork about once a month, his Korean mother-in-law comes to his home and whips it up, unasked, alongside a feast of dumplings called mandu , rice, and two-to-three containers of homemade kimchi . “I don’t want her to come over and cook, but that’s what she wants to do!” says the James Beard Award-winning chef and Momofuku alum, just the slightest bit exasperated. But Serpico, adopted by a white couple from suburban Maryland at age 2, concedes that his mother-in-law’s incessant cooking has been educational. A tremendous cook, her bulgogi is the stuff of legend. Plus, “it’s her way of showing love and making sure we’re taken care of. It’s very sweet.” Bulgogi, a classic Korean dish of thinly sliced, marinated beef, is a staple of Korean households. On January 1, 1804, Haitians declared independence from French colonial rule following the Haitian Revolution that began in 1791. Public Domain How did the scattered followers of an itinerant preacher come to form the most populous religion in the world? Tim Whitmarsh—a classicist at the University of Cambridge and author of magisterial books about empire, the early novel and more—offers a compelling answer in his new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity. To wit, Christianity took much of its shape from the cult of Augustus, first emperor of Rome. The Augustan age saw a unique revolution that redefined authority, space and literature, remaking both the inner world and the outer. Augustus drew on centuries-old Roman prophecies to cast himself as the promised one . According to his propaganda, Italy experienced auguries and miracles at Augustus’ nativity; Augustus was declared a descendant of Rome’s mythical founder, Aeneas, and therefore of the gods, and he promised to renew Roman liberty from the decadence of the late Republic. As Whitmarsh writes: “The new world was presented as the fulfillment of all the best ideals of the old.” Just so, Jesus’s birth was claimed as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies about a coming emissary of God on Earth, and this novel form of monotheism was simultaneously cast as the fruition of the Hebrew faith. pages.text: A Famous Portrait of Anne Boleyn Hides a Strange Secret | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE A Famous Portrait of Anne Boleyn Hides a Strange Secret A scientific analysis of the Hever Rose portrait has revealed a curious choice by its artist—one that hints at a vicious battle over the legitimacy of Boleyn's daughter, Queen Elizabeth I. Anne Boleyn's detractors accused her of immorality and hinted that she had the features of a witch. The Hever Rose portrait, pictured here, may have been created to refute those claims. Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy By Kelly Faircloth Published November 13, 2026 It’s one of the most famous images of one of history’s most infamous women: The “Hever Rose” portrait of Anne Boleyn depicts the controversial figure for whom England’s King Henry VIII broke with Papal Rome. Pale against a dark background and her own dark attire, Boleyn’s face is poised, almost grave; her sleek hair is half-covered by one of her iconic French hoods and her “B” pendant gleams at her neck. She holds a rose,an important Tudor emblem, delicately at her breast. In fact, she’s holding the rose a bit oddly, clasped between thumb and forefinger. All ten fingers are immediately visible against the rich fabric of her gown. It’s not how most people would instinctively hold a rose. As it turns out, there may be a reason for the prominence of her hands in the painting—one that speaks to rumors which dogged Boleyn even after her death, and which threatened the legitimacy of her daughter, Queen Elizabeth I. Photograph by Inge Johnsson, Alamy TRAVEL Big Bend Hosts the Most Bird Species of Any National Park This remote Texas park is home to a remarkable diversity of life. Published November 5, 2009 • 3 min read Location: Texas Established: June 12, 1944 Size: 801,163 acres Chihuahuan Desert vegetation—bunchgrasses, creosote bushes, cactuses, lechuguillas, yuccas, sotols, and more—covers most of the terrain. But the Rio Grande and its lush floodplains and steep, narrow canyons form almost a park of their own. So do the Chisos Mountains; up to 20 degrees cooler than the desert floor, they harbor pine, juniper, and oak, as well as deer, mountain lions, bears, and other wildlife. A heavy rain transforms the desert: Normally dry creek beds roar with water, and seeds long dormant burst into fields of wildflowers. The rocks of Big Bend are a complex lot. Two seas, one after another, flowed and subsided in the region hundreds of millions of years ago, leaving thick deposits of limestone and shale. The present mountains, except the Chisos, uplifted along with the Rockies, roughly 75 million years ago. Around the same time, a 40-mile-wide trough—most of the present-day park—sank along fault lines, leaving the cliffs of Santa Elena Canyon to the west and the Sierra del Carmen to the east rising 1,500 feet and more above the desert floor. A Paris native who’s been a resident of Marseille for over 20 years, she leads me down streets hastily sprayed with calls for strike action, to reach the grand, climate-conscious mural Man vs Wild. It has a glittering harbour, magnificent seafood and easy access to the rugged beauty of nearby Calanques National Park. pages.text: A historic guide to San Marino | National Geographic Paid content for Visit San Marino By Julia Buckley Published June 4, 2026 Perched on the aptly named Monte Titano, or Mount Titan, the landlocked city-state of San Marino enjoys spectacular views. Everywhere you look, there’s 360-degree panoramas of the rolling hills of Emilia-Romagna and the Marche regions, cascading down to the Adriatic Sea. While the ravishing landscapes of this part of the peninsula haven’t changed, history has waged major upheaval: over the centuries, the surrounding regions have gone from independent states to occupied territories and, finally, a unified Italy. San Marino however, sat on its eyrie, has remained above the fray — one of Europe’s oldest (and smallest) republics, its borders haven’t changed since 1463. Visitors often include a visit to San Marino as part of a wider trip to Italy, but while curiosity is often what lures people up Monte Titano, it’s the remarkable history that makes them stay. Its warren of medieval streets blend Renaissance, early modern and 20th-century architecture, while a trio of towers top the mountain peak. Here’s how to navigate San Marino’s layers of proud history. San Marino's medieval streets look as though they've been untouched for centuries, with steep, winding alleys and tiny piazzas. A dozen bold Afghan stallions, lashed to frenzy, collided in combat around the headless goat sprawled in the dust. These were fighting horses, giants 17 hands high, trained to kick and bite. Scientists say the Kelvin wave could be dangerous for people—and deadly for wildlife—as it travels up the California coast. Last month, around 20 homes were evacuated in Long Beach, California after heavy surf caused flooding. A blob of warm water known as a Kelvin wave is exacerbating coastal flooding caused by warmer waters, storms, and rising seas. Mario Tama, Getty Images By Ruby Mellen Published October 6, 2026 Sea levels across the west coasts of the Americas are rising after a massive bulge of water, driven by wind changes and a warmer ocean, inched its way east along the equator and along the coasts. The phenomenon, called a Kelvin wave, has officials bracing for storm surges, erosion, and transformations in marine life. Networks of satellites and buoys across the ocean have been tracking the pulse of water, which arrived on Southern California’s coast last week and will continue north. These hominins, shorter and stockier than modern humans, inhabited areas from Western Europe to Central Asia, and archaeological finds reveal that the Neanderthals were remarkably resourceful. They made stone tools, hunted large animals, used fire, wore clothing, and engaged in some symbolic behaviors, possibly even burying their dead. pages.text: A new paradigm for publishing library collections: Institutional Books 1.0, a 242B token dataset – Open Source Initiative A new paradigm for publishing library collections: Institutional Books 1.0, a 242B token dataset Part of the Deep Dive: Data Governance Webinar Series Data plays a critical role in the AI ecosystem, so much so that some model-makers have begun contacting libraries in search of new data and scraping their websites with such frequency that their ability to deliver services to their traditional patrons is impacted. A new paradigm for publishing library collections is needed to respond to the rapid development of LLMs and the resulting scarcity of high-quality, open training data. Non-Profit Bylaws ¶ As a Delaware, US-based membership corporation and an IRS registered 501(c)(3) non-profit, the ASF is governed by a set of corporate bylaws. pages.text: A Soviet Ghost Town in the Arctic Circle, Pyramiden Stands Alone Skip to main content The northernmost statue of Lenin. Photo: Rachel Nuwer People say that the Soviet town of Pyramiden was abandoned overnight. In reality, however, the desertion occurred over a period of months. But a visitor arriving in Pyramiden in the fall of 1998 would be justified in reaching that conclusion. In the newly emptied town, withering plants sat on windowsills; clean dishes were stacked on the cafeteria shelves; and neatly folded sheets rested on the former residents’ beds. The equipment used for coal mining—the town’s raison d’être—sat where workers had left it, ready to rev back into action at the push of a button. It was as if several hundred people had abruptly stopped what they were doing and simply walked away. The residents, however, never returned, and today the town still stands much as it was when the last men departed. Located in Svalbard , an archipelago situated between Norway and the North Pole, Pyramiden can be reached by boat from about mid-May until the beginning of October, when waters bordering the town are free from sea ice. But throughout the cold winter months—three of which are engulfed by 24-hour darkness—Pyramiden hosts only the occasional stray polar bear. To explore Pyramiden is to step back in time, to the heyday of the USSR. Soviet culture, architecture and politics permeate the town, from the block-style housing to the bust of Lenin—the world’s northernmost statue of that communist revolutionary—gazing down, fatherly and proud, on Pyramiden’s main square. Turnley Published April 21, 2026 This story originally published in the February 1990 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . The mighty inland sea lies stricken now, caught in the grip of some evil chemistry as its waters dry to salt and blow away as noxious dust to strike the people with illness and death. It has never happened before within the time frame of a single generation, the disappearance of such a large body of water; but the Soviet Union's Aral Sea, once larger in area than any of the Great Lakes save Superior, is vanishing from the face of the earth. As the waters continue to recede, final destruction of the Aral—26,000 square miles in 1960—could occur before another 30 years have passed. The desiccation is taking place not only at a rapid pace but also with stealth, and in silence: the way a stallion plunges his muzzle into a bucket of water and drains it. pages.text: A Stunning Escape From Slavery Told on Tattered Pages Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images from Anastasiia Hevko via Adobe Stock / Collection of the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture / Cindy Elder In the mid-1800s, before the Civil War, Thomas White fled his enslavement in Maryland for freedom. It was a risky escape, one that involved a horseback ride under the cover of darkness, abolitionists helping to hide him, and a northward journey through Delaware and Pennsylvania. Ultimately, he arrived—safe and free—in Massachusetts. The details of White’s flight are chronicled on 40-odd sheets of paper and were written most probably by other people who heard his story. Such slave narratives are exceedingly rare, and this one’s length made it especially unique. Smithsonian magazine wrote about the discovery last year. In this episode, we speak with Rachel Fortuna Cabral, the Roger Williams University undergraduate who helped study the manuscript, and scholar Deborah Plant to learn about White’s escape, how the papers were discovered, and what such narratives tell us about slavery and emancipation in the United States. By Ben Goldfarb Photographs by Robin Hammond Published September 23, 2026 In spring 2020, as COVID-19 erupted worldwide, Gladys Kalema-Zikusoka feared less for her own health than for the mountain gorillas in Bwindi Impenetrable National Park , 120 square miles of misty rainforest in Uganda’s southwest corner. Around 40,000 tourists visit Bwindi annually, bearing pathogens from around the world. In 2009 a pair of Rwandan gorillas died from a respiratory virus likely transmitted by a tourist, and Kalema-Zikusoka, a Ugandan wildlife veterinarian, knew that the coronavirus posed an even greater threat. “A lot of [tourists] are so excited to see [gorillas] that they won’t tell you that they’re sick,” she says. As the pandemic spread around the world, Kalema-Zikusoka—who serves as executive director of Conservation Through Public Health , an organization dedicated to protecting mountain gorillas—instructed anyone who came close to the primates to wear masks. As temperatures soared into the mid-90s during Europe’s heat wave, I packed my bags and embarked on a six-hour road trip from Switzerland to Liguria. Rather than seeking out seasonal treats like granita or gelato, I was headed to the Italian coast for focaccia. When most Americans­—and Italians, for that matter—think of focaccia, they think of the pillowy-soft version that’s leavened with yeast, baked in a sheet pan and perfect for scarpetta , or the mopping up of delicious sauces. However, ask any Ligurian, and they will tell you that the focaccia that reigns supreme is focaccia di Recco. Focaccia di Recco is a specialty dish in Liguria.
